intro: Every sport leaves paper behind. Clubs write constitutions. Committees vote on rules and print them in yearly editions. Leagues keep minutes of their meetings. Fans save scorebooks, tickets and programs. Architects draw plans for fields and stands. Each of these papers carries a date and the name of the person or body that made it.

In this unit, you pick up one sport's papers and read them as a historian does. You will follow the Football Association from its 1863 meeting in London, the National League from its 1876 constitution, and college football from the crisis of 1905. You will read the 1867 baseball report that shut out Black clubs and the 1921 resolution that closed English grounds to women's teams. Then you will visit the halls and archives that keep sport's objects, from Cooperstown in 1939 to Kansas City in 1990.

By the end, you will be able to name the body behind a rule, date it, and say who it let in or kept out. You will be able to tell a record made at the time from a legend told later. You will also be able to write a clear caption for a sports object: what it is, who made it, when, and how it reached the collection.
bigQuestion: What can one sport's papers and objects prove about who held power in it, and who was written out?

chapters.title: Pick One Sport and Its Paper
chapters.bigQuestion: What can the written papers of one sport tell us about who made its rules and who was kept out?

story.title: A Stack on the Library Desk
story.kicker: One student lays out one sport's founding papers in order and sees a pattern.
paragraphs: It is a gray afternoon at a public library in Chicago. A senior named Dana sits at a long table with a stack of photocopies. Every page comes from one sport: baseball. She has sorted them by year, oldest on top. A librarian has helped her find each one in books of reprinted documents and in online archives.

The top page is a short list of rules from the Knickerbocker Base Ball Club of New York, dated 1845. Under it lies a report from the National Association of Base Ball Players, dated December 1867. Next comes the constitution of the National League, written in 1876 by club owners who met at a hotel in New York. A Chicago man, William Hulbert, led that meeting.

Farther down the stack is a paper from February 1920. It records the founding of the Negro National League at a YMCA in Kansas City, Missouri. Rube Foster, owner of the Chicago American Giants, called that meeting. Near the bottom sits a news release from December 2020. In it, Major League Baseball says it now counts seven Negro Leagues as major leagues.

Dana reads the 1867 report twice. It says the national association should turn away any club with Black members. She checks the 1876 constitution. It says nothing about race at all. Yet no Black player appeared in the National League for decades. She writes a note in her margin: some lines are written down, and some are kept without being written.

By closing time, Dana has a timeline taped across two pages. Each date has a name beside it: a club, a league, a committee or a company. She can now say who wrote each rule, when, and who it left out. Her stack of paper has become the start of a history.
story.think: Why might a rule that was never written down be harder to prove than one that was?

lessons.title: Two Kinds of Paper
lessons.mainIdea: Most sports bodies keep two kinds of paper: a constitution that sets up the body and a rule book that sets out the game.
reading: On 26 October 1863, men from about a dozen London clubs and schools met at the Freemasons' Tavern on Great Queen Street. They formed the Football Association, or FA. Ebenezer Cobb Morley, a lawyer, served as its first secretary. The meeting set up the body first: its name, its members and how it would vote.

Over the next six weeks, the members argued about the game itself. On 8 December 1863, they adopted thirteen written Laws of the Game. The Laws banned carrying the ball in the hands and banned hacking, which meant kicking an opponent's shins. The Blackheath club disagreed and left. In 1871, clubs that wanted handling formed the Rugby Football Union.

The FA's story shows two different kinds of paper. A *constitution* sets up a body: who may join, who leads, how votes are counted and how money is handled. The *bylaws* of a body add detailed rules for running the body's meetings. A *rule book* is different. It sets out how the game is scored, how long it lasts and what is allowed on the field.

A historian studying one sport needs both. The constitution tells who held power. The rule book tells what that power produced. A change in either one leaves a date on paper, and each date can be checked. London sporting newspapers reported the 1863 meetings, giving historians a second record to check against the FA's own.

words.d: the founding document of a body; it says who may join, who leads and how decisions are made
detailed rules for running a body's meetings, officers and money
the written rules of the game itself: scoring, time and what is allowed
the governing body of football in England, founded in London on 26 October 1863

lessons.title: A League Written in 1876
lessons.mainIdea: The 1876 National League constitution put club owners, not players, in charge of professional baseball.
reading: On 2 February 1876, representatives of eight baseball clubs met at the Grand Central Hotel in New York City. William Hulbert, an officer of the Chicago White Stockings, had called them together. They formed the National League of Professional Base Ball Clubs. Morgan Bulkeley of Hartford became its first president, and Hulbert soon followed him.

The older National Association of Professional Base Ball Players, founded in 1871, had been run largely by players. Clubs came and went, and many games were thought to be fixed by gamblers. The new league's constitution made the *club*, not the player, the member. Owners held the votes. Each member club had to come from a city of at least 75,000 people.

The constitution also banned gambling by players and club officers. In 1877, the league expelled four Louisville players for throwing games. Later rules barred Sunday games and the sale of alcohol at league parks. When Cincinnati sold beer and rented its grounds on Sundays, the league pushed it out after the 1880 season.

The document shaped what came next. In 1882, a rival called the American Association formed. It sold beer and charged 25 cents a ticket, half the National League's usual 50 cents. The two leagues show how a *charter*, a founding paper that grants a group its powers, can decide who can afford a seat as well as who can play.

words.d: in early professional baseball, the business that owned a team and held a vote in the league
a founding paper that creates a group and grants it powers
the professional baseball league founded in New York on 2 February 1876
to force a member out of a group by a vote

lessons.title: Rules Put Into Print
lessons.mainIdea: Many modern sports can be dated from the year their rules were first written down and printed.
reading: Before printing, most games followed local custom. Each village, school or club played its own way. When teams from different places met, they first had to agree on rules. Writing the rules down made it possible for strangers to play the same game. In England, public schools such as Eton, Harrow and Rugby each kept their own football rules.

In New York, the Knickerbocker Base Ball Club wrote down a list of twenty rules in September 1845. In London, the FA printed its Laws in December 1863. In 1867, a Welsh sportsman named John Graham Chambers wrote a set of boxing rules. They were published under the name of the Marquess of Queensberry, who supported them. These are called the *Queensberry Rules*.

In December 1891, James Naismith wrote thirteen rules for a new game at the YMCA International Training School in Springfield, Massachusetts. On 15 January 1892, the school's newspaper, *The Triangle*, printed them. YMCA branches across the country read that paper. Within a few years, basketball was being played far from Springfield.

A printed rule is a *primary source*: a record made at the time by the people involved. A later story about the rules is a *secondary source*. Historians trust a printed date more than a memory, because the paper can be seen and checked. A modern textbook chapter about Naismith's rules is a secondary source.

words.d: boxing rules written by John Graham Chambers and published in 1867 under the Marquess of Queensberry's name
the newspaper of the YMCA training school in Springfield, which printed Naismith's basketball rules in January 1892
a record made at the time by people who were there, such as a printed rule book or meeting minutes
a later account written by someone studying the past

check.why: John Graham Chambers wrote them; they were published in 1867 under the Marquess of Queensberry's name.

check.q: Which is a primary source about early basketball?

lessons.title: Who May Change a Law
lessons.mainIdea: Since 1886, only the International Football Association Board can change soccer's Laws of the Game.
reading: England, Scotland, Wales and Ireland had each set up a separate football association by the 1880s. Their rules did not fully match. When their teams met, arguments followed. On 2 June 1886, the four associations held the first meeting of the *International Football Association Board*, or IFAB, in London.

The IFAB became the only body that could change the Laws. A change needed a large majority of votes. This made the Laws slow to change and hard for one country to control. FIFA, founded in Paris on 21 May 1904 by seven European associations, joined the IFAB in 1913.

Today the IFAB has four British votes and four FIFA votes. A change needs six of the eight. That rule means neither side can change the game alone. The IFAB meets each year at its *annual general meeting*, and new Laws usually take effect on 1 July. FIFA's four votes speak for all of its member nations together.

For a historian, this structure is useful. Every change to soccer's Laws has a meeting, a year and a body attached to it. A student can trace when a rule appeared by reading the IFAB's yearly editions of the Laws of the Game. The Laws have been revised many times; a major rewrite in 2016 made the text shorter and clearer.

words.d: IFAB; the body, formed in 1886, that alone can change soccer's Laws of the Game
the world governing body of soccer, founded in Paris in 1904
a yearly meeting where a body's members vote on changes
more than half of the votes; some bodies require a larger share for big changes

look.title: Eight Seats at One Table
look.text: Picture a meeting room. Four seats belong to the football associations of England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Four belong to FIFA, which speaks for more than two hundred national associations. A proposal to change a Law needs six votes to pass.
look.prompt: Why might the four British associations still hold half the votes? What does that tell you about where the Laws were first written?

check.q: In what year did the IFAB first meet?
check.why: The four British associations held the IFAB's first meeting in London on 2 June 1886.

check.q: How many of the eight IFAB votes does a change to the Laws need?
check.why: A change needs six of eight votes, so neither the British side nor FIFA can act alone.

check.q: Where was FIFA founded in 1904?
check.why: Seven European associations founded FIFA in Paris on 21 May 1904.

lessons.title: A Crisis Writes New Rules
lessons.mainIdea: Deaths and injuries in college football in 1905 led to a new national body in 1906, which became the NCAA.
reading: College football in 1905 was rough and often deadly. Newspapers counted about eighteen deaths that season, many of them among young players. Columbia was among the colleges that gave up football. Others threatened to. In October 1905, President Theodore Roosevelt invited coaches and officials from Harvard, Yale and Princeton to the White House to discuss the game.

After a player died in a game between Union College and New York University that November, NYU chancellor Henry MacCracken called a meeting of colleges. On 31 March 1906, sixty-two schools founded the *Intercollegiate Athletic Association of the United States*, or IAAUS. In 1910, it took a new name: the National Collegiate Athletic Association, or *NCAA*.

The 1906 rules committee made changes that are still named in histories of the game. It legalized the forward pass and raised the distance needed for a first down from five yards to ten. These rules were meant to open up play and reduce the crushing mass of bodies in the middle of the field.

The paper trail here is rich. There are newspaper death counts, White House records, meeting minutes and the rule books of 1906. Together they show how public pressure produced a new *governing body* and new written rules in less than a year. At first the IAAUS mainly made rules. Its first national championship, in track and field, came in 1921.

words.w: Intercollegiate Athletic Association of the United States
words.d: IAAUS; the body of 62 colleges founded on 31 March 1906; renamed the NCAA in 1910
National Collegiate Athletic Association; the governing body for many U.S. college sports
an organization with the power to set rules and run competitions for a sport
a group chosen by a governing body to write and change the rules of the game

look.title: Three Papers From One Winter
look.text: Paper one: a newspaper table from November 1905 listing players who died that season. Paper two: a White House guest list from October 1905 naming football men from three colleges. Paper three: minutes of a New York meeting in March 1906 listing sixty-two member schools.
look.prompt: Put these papers in order and explain how each one led to the next.

check.why: Theodore Roosevelt invited Harvard, Yale and Princeton football leaders in October 1905.

check.q: What did the IAAUS become in 1910?
check.why: The IAAUS, founded in 1906, took the name National Collegiate Athletic Association in 1910.

check.why: The forward pass became legal under the 1906 college rules.

lessons.title: Rules for High Schools
lessons.mainIdea: State associations like the IHSA, founded in 1900, and a national federation formed in Chicago in 1920 wrote rules for high school sport.
reading: In the late 1800s, high school teams were often run by students. Some teams used older players who were not enrolled. Principals worried about fairness and schoolwork. In Illinois, principals formed a state body in 1900. Today it is called the Illinois High School Association, or *IHSA*.

The IHSA wrote *eligibility* rules. These decide who may play: a player had to be a student, passing classes and under an age limit. The IHSA also ran state tournaments. Its first boys' tennis state champion was crowned in 1912. Its boys' wrestling state series began in 1937.

State associations soon wanted to work together. On 14 May 1920, L. W. Smith, the secretary of the Illinois association, hosted a meeting in Chicago. Representatives came from Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Michigan and Wisconsin. They formed the group that became the *National Federation of State High School Associations*, or NFHS.

Over time, the NFHS began writing its own rule books for high school sports. Today it publishes rule books for many sports, used by high schools across the country. A student studying one sport can compare the NFHS rules with the NCAA's college rules and a pro league's rules. The three rule books often differ, and each difference has a date.

words.d: Illinois High School Association; the body founded in 1900 that runs high school sport in Illinois
the rules that decide who may take part in a sport

words.w: National Federation of State High School Associations
words.d: NFHS; the national group of state school associations, begun at a Chicago meeting in 1920
a set of tournaments run by a state association that ends in a state championship

choices: rules about the size of the field

check.why: L. W. Smith of the Illinois association hosted the meeting in Chicago on 14 May 1920.

check.q: In what year was the IHSA founded?
check.why: The IHSA was founded in 1900; 1912 and 1937 are dates of its first tennis and wrestling champions.

lessons.title: The December 1867 Report
lessons.mainIdea: In 1867, a committee of the national baseball association wrote that clubs with Black members should be turned away.
reading: The National Association of Base Ball Players held its first convention in New York in 1857. It began with clubs from the New York area. By 1867 its member clubs came from many states, including Pennsylvania. Each year, a *nominating committee* reviewed which clubs could join.

The Pythian Base Ball Club of Philadelphia was a Black club led by Octavius Catto, a teacher and civil rights leader. In October 1867, the Pythians applied to the Pennsylvania state baseball association. Their delegate learned they would be voted down and withdrew the application.

At the national convention in December 1867, the nominating committee issued its report. It said the association should not admit any club that had one or more Black members. The committee wrote that it hoped to keep politics out of the association. The report put the exclusion into the association's official record.

Catto kept fighting for equal rights in Philadelphia. On 10 October 1871, election day, he was shot and killed on a Philadelphia street. The 1867 report is a primary source that historians use to date the first written *color line* in organized baseball.

words.d: a small group that reviews who may join a body and reports to the full membership
a rule or practice that kept Black people out of teams, leagues or places
a Black baseball club in Philadelphia led by Octavius Catto after the Civil War
a large meeting of a body's members to vote on its business

look.text: The committee recommends that no club with one or more colored persons be admitted. It says this is to keep out of the association any question that might cause division.
look.cite: Report of the Nominating Committee, National Association of Base Ball Players, annual convention, December 1867
look.prompt: What reason did the committee give for the exclusion? What does that reason leave unsaid?

check.why: Octavius Catto, a teacher and civil rights leader, led the Pythians.

check.q: What did the December 1867 nominating committee report recommend?
choices: that clubs with Black members not be admitted

check.why: The report said no club with one or more Black members should be admitted.

lessons.title: Lines Nobody Signed
lessons.mainIdea: Most of professional sport's color lines were unwritten agreements, so their start and end are dated by who played, not by a rule.
reading: In 1884, Moses Fleetwood Walker caught for the Toledo Blue Stockings of the American Association, then a major league. His brother Weldy also played a few games. In July 1887, the directors of the minor International League voted to approve no new contracts with Black players. After that, Black players were pushed out of white professional baseball.

No major league ever printed a rule against Black players. Owners simply did not sign them. Historians call this kind of exclusion an *unwritten rule* or a *gentlemen's agreement*. Because it was never written, its end is dated by a player's first game, not by a vote.

Black players built their own institutions. On 13 February 1920, Rube Foster and other owners met at the Paseo YMCA in Kansas City, Missouri. They founded the *Negro National League*. Foster owned and managed the Chicago American Giants. Other Negro leagues followed in the 1920s and 1930s.

Jackie Robinson played his first game for the Brooklyn Dodgers on 15 April 1947. In other leagues, the dates differ. Kenny Washington and Woody Strode joined the Los Angeles Rams in 1946. Earl Lloyd played in the NBA in 1950, and Willie O'Ree skated for the Boston Bruins in 1958.

words.d: a practice everyone in a group follows even though it appears in no document
an unwritten understanding among powerful people, such as owners agreeing not to sign Black players
the Black baseball league founded by Rube Foster and other owners in Kansas City on 13 February 1920
opening a team, league or place to people who were kept out, especially by race

check.q: What did the International League directors vote in July 1887?
choices: to approve no new contracts with Black players
check.why: The directors voted to approve no new contracts with Black players, helping push them out.

check.q: Where was the Negro National League founded in 1920?
choices: at a hotel in New York
at the Paseo YMCA in Kansas City
check.why: Rube Foster and other owners met at the Paseo YMCA in Kansas City on 13 February 1920.

check.q: Why is the end of the major league color line dated by Jackie Robinson's first game?

because the league printed a new rule that day

check.why: The color line was an unwritten agreement, so its end is dated by who played, not by a vote.

lessons.title: A Ban on Women's Football
lessons.mainIdea: On 5 December 1921, the FA banned women's football from its members' grounds, and the ban lasted fifty years.
reading: During the First World War, women worked in British factories that made weapons and supplies. Many factories formed women's football teams. The best known came from the Dick, Kerr and Company works in Preston. On Boxing Day 1920, the *Dick, Kerr Ladies* drew about 53,000 people to Goodison Park in Liverpool.

Women's matches often raised money for charity and for wounded soldiers. On 5 December 1921, the FA council passed a resolution. It said football was unsuitable for women and should not be encouraged. It asked its member clubs not to let women's teams use their grounds.

The ban did not forbid women from playing. It closed the large stadiums, the paid officials and the crowds. Women's teams had to play on rougher public fields. The *resolution* stayed in force for fifty years. Some teams kept touring. In 1922 the Dick, Kerr Ladies traveled to the United States and played men's teams there.

In 1969, the Women's Football Association formed in England. The FA lifted its ban in 1971. The paper trail runs from the council's minutes of 1921 to the vote of 1971. Both dates are in the FA's own records, which makes this exclusion easy to cite. In 2022, England's women won the European Championship at Wembley Stadium.

words.d: a formal decision voted on and recorded by a body's council or members
a women's football team from a factory in Preston, England, that drew huge crowds around 1920
the group of elected leaders who make decisions for a governing body
an official order that forbids something

look.title: The FA Council, December 1921
look.text: The council believes the game of football is not suitable for women and should not be encouraged. It asks clubs belonging to the Association not to allow their grounds to be used for women's matches.
look.cite: Football Association, resolution of the council, 5 December 1921
look.prompt: The resolution did not tell women to stop playing. How could it still shut them out?

check.q: About how many people watched the Dick, Kerr Ladies at Goodison Park on Boxing Day 1920?
check.why: About 53,000 people came to Goodison Park to watch them.

check.q: What did the FA's 1921 resolution do?
choices: It made women's football illegal in Britain.
It asked member clubs not to let women's teams use their grounds.
It gave women seats on the council.
check.why: The resolution closed members' grounds to women's teams; it did not make playing illegal.

check.q: When did the FA lift its ban on women's football?
check.why: The Women's Football Association formed in 1969, and the FA lifted the ban in 1971.

lessons.title: Memory Versus Minutes
lessons.mainIdea: Records made at the time are stronger evidence than stories told decades later, and some famous origin stories are legends.
reading: In 1905, the sporting goods maker Albert Spalding set up a panel to decide where baseball came from. It was led by Abraham G. Mills, a former National League president, and is known as the *Mills Commission*. Spalding wanted baseball to be seen as purely American, not as a child of the English game rounders.

The commission's report, dated 30 December 1907, named Abner Doubleday as the inventor of baseball in Cooperstown, New York, in 1839. Its main evidence was a letter from a mining engineer named Abner Graves, who recalled events from his boyhood. Doubleday was a cadet at West Point in 1839. He never claimed to have invented baseball. Historians treat the Doubleday story as a *legend*.

Naismith's case is different. His rules were printed in January 1892, weeks after the first game. Almost fifty years later, he wrote a book, Basketball: Its Origin and Development, published in 1941 after his death in 1939. The book is a *memoir*, a personal account written from memory.

Historians use both kinds of papers but weigh them differently. The 1892 print is strong evidence about the first rules. The 1941 memoir tells what Naismith remembered and believed. When a memory and a record disagree, the record made at the time usually wins.

words.d: a panel set up in 1905 that in 1907 wrongly named Abner Doubleday as the inventor of baseball
a traditional story told as history that records do not support
a personal account of past events written from the writer's own memory
to support a claim with a second, independent piece of evidence

look.title: Two Claims, Two Kinds of Proof
look.text: Claim A: Baseball was invented by Abner Doubleday in Cooperstown in 1839. Evidence: a letter written in 1905 by a man recalling his childhood. Claim B: Basketball's first rules numbered thirteen. Evidence: a school newspaper printed on 15 January 1892.
look.prompt: Which claim is better supported? What would a historian need to corroborate the weaker one?

check.q: What did the Mills Commission's 1907 report claim?
choices: that Abner Doubleday invented baseball in 1839
check.why: The report named Doubleday and Cooperstown, a claim historians now call a legend.

check.q: Where was Abner Doubleday in 1839?
check.why: Doubleday was a cadet at West Point in 1839, one reason historians reject the story.

check.q: Why is Naismith's 1941 book called a memoir?
choices: It is a set of meeting minutes.
It was written by a committee.
It is his personal account written from memory decades later.
check.why: A memoir is a personal account from memory; Naismith wrote it nearly fifty years after the first game.

lessons.title: Naming the Body and the Year
lessons.mainIdea: A good citation of a sports document names the body that issued it, the document's title and its year or edition.
reading: Rule books change often, so the year matters. The IFAB publishes a new edition of the Laws of the Game each year. Major League Baseball publishes the Official Baseball Rules with a year on the cover. A rule quoted from the 1950 edition may not be in the 2020 edition. A *citation* must say which one.

Laws have dates too. President Richard Nixon signed the Education Amendments of 1972 on 23 June 1972. *Title IX* is one section of that law. It bars sex discrimination in education programs that receive federal money. The government's detailed regulations explaining how Title IX applied to school sports came later, in 1975.

The body matters as much as the date. Different bodies govern different levels of the same sport. A high school game in Illinois follows rules adopted by the IHSA and the NFHS. A college game follows NCAA rules. A professional game follows the league's own book. Naming the *issuing body* tells a reader whose power stood behind a rule.

Put together, a strong citation reads like this: body, title, year. For example: Football Association, council resolution, 5 December 1921. Or: National Association of Base Ball Players, nominating committee report, December 1867. Or: Education Amendments of 1972, Title IX, signed 23 June 1972.

words.d: a short note naming where a fact came from so a reader can check it
one printing of a document in a given year; rule books have a new edition when rules change
the section of the Education Amendments of 1972 that bars sex discrimination in federally funded education programs
the organization that wrote or approved a document
a detailed rule written by a government agency to explain how a law works

look.title: Fix the Citation

look.prompt: Rewrite the student's sentence so it names the body, the document and the year.

check.q: What is Title IX?
choices: a section of a 1972 law that bars sex discrimination in federally funded education
the ninth rule in Naismith's list

check.q: Why must a citation of a rule book include the year?

because the rules change from edition to edition
because the year shows the price
check.why: Rule books have new editions when rules change, so the year shows which version is meant.

check.q: Whose rules does a college game follow?
check.why: College games follow rules set by the NCAA, the college governing body.

review.q: Which document sets up a body's members, leaders and voting?
review.why: A constitution sets up the body; a rule book sets out the game.

review.q: Which city did William Hulbert's club represent when he helped found the National League?
review.why: Hulbert was an officer of the Chicago White Stockings.

review.q: Which body alone can change soccer's Laws of the Game?
review.why: Since 1886, only the International Football Association Board can change the Laws.

review.q: What pushed college leaders to form the IAAUS in 1906?
choices: deaths and injuries in the 1905 football season
review.why: Newspapers counted about eighteen deaths in 1905, which led to the new body in March 1906.

review.q: How is the December 1867 baseball report different from the color line of the 1880s to 1940s?
choices: The 1867 exclusion was written down; the later one was mostly unwritten.
The 1867 report let Black clubs join.
The later color line was printed in the National League constitution.
review.why: The 1867 committee put exclusion in writing; the later major league line was an unwritten agreement.

review.q: Which is the stronger evidence for basketball's first rules?
review.why: The rules printed in The Triangle in January 1892 were made at the time.

review.q: What happened to women's football in England between 1921 and 1971?
choices: It was the FA's top league.
It was played only in schools.

A strong citation names the body, the document and the date.

chapters.title: Objects as Evidence
chapters.bigQuestion: How can a scorebook, a ticket or a ballpark plan be read as evidence, and who decides which objects are kept?

story.title: Two Papers in One Box
story.kicker: An archivist opens a gray box and sets two very different papers side by side.
paragraphs: In a quiet reading room, an archivist lifts the lid of a gray cardboard box. The box is acid-free, which means it will not yellow the papers inside. She wears no gloves, because clean, dry hands are safer for old paper than cotton gloves. A student sits across the table with a pencil. Pens are not allowed near the papers.

The first object is a scorebook from a baseball season in the early 1900s. Its pages are ruled into small boxes. A scorer has filled each box with letters, numbers and small marks in faded ink. On the inside cover, someone has written a name and a city.

The second object is a large folded sheet of heavy paper: a ballpark plan. It shows the outline of the stands, the diamond and the fences. Numbers along the edges give distances in feet. In the lower corner, a small box names the architect's office and gives a date.

The archivist points to a card tucked into the box. It carries a catalog number, a short description and a line about where the objects came from. A family gave them to the collection decades ago. That line, she explains, is part of the evidence too.

The student looks from one paper to the other. One was made in the stands by a fan or a club scorer, one pencil mark at a time. The other was made in an office before a single seat was built. Both are records of the same game, seen from two very different places.
story.think: Why might the note about where an object came from matter as much as the object itself?

lessons.title: The Scorebook and the Box Score
lessons.mainIdea: Henry Chadwick helped turn baseball games into printed numbers, and scorebooks became records historians can read.
reading: Henry Chadwick was born in England in 1824 and moved to the United States as a boy. He grew up with cricket, which already kept detailed written scores. In the 1850s he began writing about baseball for New York newspapers. He wanted readers to see a whole game in a small space.

Around 1859, Chadwick published a *box score*: a small table listing each player and what he did in the game. He adapted it from cricket scoring. He is often credited with using the letter K to stand for a strikeout. In 1860 he edited *Beadle's Dime Base-Ball Player*, one of the first yearly baseball guides.

Newspapers printed box scores every day of the season. Clubs and fans kept their own scorebooks, bound books with a page for each game. These books recorded who played, in what order and what happened. They also often recorded the date, the weather, the ballpark and the crowd.

For a historian, a scorebook is a *primary record* of a single game. It can confirm a newspaper report or show where the paper got a fact wrong. The Baseball Hall of Fame elected Chadwick in 1938. He is still the only sportswriter enshrined there as a member rather than through a writers' award.

words.d: a small printed table that sums up each player's part in one game
a bound book in which a scorer records each game as it is played
an original account made at the time an event happened
an early yearly baseball guide, first edited by Henry Chadwick in 1860

look.title: A Page and a Newspaper
look.text: A scorebook page from a July game lists nine names for the home team in pencil. The next morning's newspaper box score lists the same nine names, but it spells one player's name differently and gives a different crowd size.
look.prompt: Which source would you trust for the spelling? Which for the crowd size? What else could you check?

check.q: Which game did Henry Chadwick borrow scorekeeping ideas from?
check.why: Chadwick grew up with cricket and adapted its detailed scoring to baseball.

check.q: What is a box score?
choices: a small table summing up each player's part in a game
the box an umpire stands in
a ticket for a box seat
a rule about the batter's box
check.why: A box score is a printed table showing what each player did.

check.q: In what year was Chadwick elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame?
check.why: Chadwick was elected in 1938 and remains the only sportswriter enshrined as a member.

lessons.title: Tickets and the Gate
lessons.mainIdea: Tickets show who paid to see a game, what it cost and, in segregated places, where each person was allowed to sit.
reading: Early baseball was played on open fields where anyone could watch for free. In 1862, William Cammeyer opened the Union Grounds in Brooklyn, New York. He built a fence around the field and charged admission. It is often called the first enclosed ballpark. The fence made the game a business, because the *gate* could now be counted.

A *ticket* is small, but it holds many facts. It usually shows a date, a price, a section and a seat. It may name the club, the league and the printer. Saved tickets let historians compare prices across years and see which seats cost the most. Paper tickets were often torn at the gate, so a saved stub is usually the fan's half.

Tickets and seating charts also record *segregation*. In many ballparks, Black fans were kept to certain sections. At Sportsman's Park in St. Louis, Black fans were limited to the pavilion and bleachers until 1944. A ticket stub from such a section is evidence of a rule that kept people apart.

Tickets can also show who paid for a stadium and who profited. A stub may carry a tax line or a charity line. Collected together, stubs from one team over many years show how the gate grew and who could afford it. Many clubs now sell digital tickets, so paper stubs from recent seasons are becoming rare.

words.d: the money a club takes in from people paying to enter a game
a printed pass that lets a person into an event; it often shows date, price and seat
separating people by race, through laws or long-held customs
a field with a fence around it, so that the owner can charge admission

look.title: A Stub in a Drawer
look.text: A ticket stub from the 1930s reads: Sportsman's Park, St. Louis. Pavilion. General admission. It shows a price and a date, but no seat number. On the back, someone has written the name of a Negro League star who was in town that week.
look.prompt: What can this stub tell you about the fan who held it and about the ballpark's rules?

check.q: Who opened the Union Grounds in Brooklyn in 1862?
check.why: William Cammeyer fenced the Union Grounds and charged admission in 1862.

check.q: What does the gate mean in sports business?
choices: the money taken in from paying fans
the office where rules are kept
check.why: The gate is the money a club takes in from admission.

check.q: Until what year were Black fans limited to certain sections at Sportsman's Park in St. Louis?
check.why: Sportsman's Park limited Black fans to the pavilion and bleachers until 1944.

lessons.title: Guides and Official Reports
lessons.mainIdea: Yearly guides and official reports gather rules, results and records into one printed place that historians can cite.
reading: After 1876, Albert Spalding's sporting goods company printed a yearly baseball guide. Henry Chadwick edited Spalding's Official Base Ball Guide for many years, until his death in 1908. Each edition held the season's rules, standings and records. Spalding's company also printed guides for football, basketball and other sports.

A *guide* was part rule book and part advertisement. Its pages sold Spalding bats, balls and uniforms. That mix matters to a historian. It shows that the company printing the rules also sold the equipment the rules required. For decades, Spalding also made the official ball of the National League.

The Olympic Games have their own printed record. The organizing committee of each Games publishes an *official report*. It lists the events, the athletes, the results, the budget and the buildings. The reports go back to the first modern Games in Athens in 1896.

Many official reports have been scanned and put online. The LA84 Foundation in Los Angeles, created with money left over from the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics, keeps a large sports library. A student can read a report from a Games held a century ago, word for word.

words.d: a yearly printed book holding a sport's rules, records and results
the printed record an Olympic organizing committee publishes about its Games
the group in a host city that plans and runs one Olympic Games
a Los Angeles sports foundation funded by the 1984 Olympic surplus that keeps a large sports library

look.title: An Official Report's Contents
look.text: The report of each Olympic Games names the organizing committee, lists every sport and event, gives results for every athlete, and describes the stadiums, the budget and the ceremonies.
look.cite: Official Reports of the Olympic Games, 1896 onward, LA84 Foundation Digital Library
look.prompt: Which part of an official report would help you study who was allowed to compete?

check.q: Who edited Spalding's Official Base Ball Guide for many years?
check.why: Henry Chadwick edited the Spalding guide until his death in 1908.

check.q: Why does a historian care that Spalding's guides included advertisements?
choices: The company printing the rules also sold the gear the rules required.
Ads were banned by the National League.
Ads show the scores of games.
check.why: The mix shows a link between the rule book and the equipment business.

check.q: What does an Olympic organizing committee publish after its Games?
choices: a rule book for every sport
check.why: Each organizing committee publishes an official report of its Games.

lessons.title: Thirteen Rules, Two Pages
lessons.mainIdea: Naismith's original typed rules became a famous object, sold at auction in 2010 and now shown in Kansas.
reading: The thirteen rules James Naismith wrote in December 1891 survive as two typed pages. They stayed with the Naismith family for more than a century. They are the oldest known copy of basketball's rules. As a *physical object*, they are different from the printed copy in The Triangle.

On 10 December 2010, the auction house Sotheby's sold the two pages in New York. The buyer was David Booth, a businessman who had studied at the University of Kansas. He paid about $4.3 million. Booth was born in Kansas and later founded an investment firm.

Booth gave the rules to the University of Kansas in Lawrence. Naismith had coached basketball there from 1898 to 1907 and taught at the school for nearly forty years. The pages are now displayed on the Kansas campus in Lawrence, where Naismith is also buried.

The story of these pages is a lesson in *provenance*, the record of who owned an object and when. Each owner, from Naismith to his family to the auction to the university, is part of the object's history. A museum label that names that chain helps visitors trust the object is real.

words.d: a real thing that can be held and examined, such as a typed page, a ball or a ticket
the record of who owned an object and when, from its maker to today
a public sale where buyers bid against each other and the highest bid wins
a gift given to a museum, school or library

look.title: The Path of Naismith's Rules
look.cite: The Triangle, 15 January 1892; University of Kansas records; Sotheby's sale, New York, 10 December 2010
look.prompt: How many years did the typed pages stay in private hands before the auction?

check.q: What auction house sold Naismith's original rules in 2010?
check.why: Sotheby's sold the two typed pages in New York on 10 December 2010.

check.q: What is provenance?
choices: the record of who owned an object and when
the price paid at an auction
the place where a game was played
check.why: Provenance is the chain of ownership of an object from its maker to today.

check.q: Why did David Booth give the rules to the University of Kansas?
choices: Naismith had coached and taught there, and Booth had studied there.
check.why: Naismith coached at Kansas from 1898 to 1907, and Booth was a former Kansas student.

lessons.title: A Ballpark on Paper
lessons.mainIdea: Architects' plans record how a venue was meant to be built, who it was built for and when it changed.
reading: Every ballpark and arena begins as a drawing. An *architectural plan* shows the outline of the building from above. An *elevation* shows it from the side. Plans carry dimensions, materials, seat counts and the architect's name and date. Older copies of plans were often blueprints, printed as white lines on blue paper.

In Chicago, one architect designed two of the city's most famous ballparks. Zachary Taylor Davis designed Comiskey Park for the White Sox, which opened on 1 July 1910. He also designed Weeghman Park, which opened on 23 April 1914 for the Chicago Whales of the Federal League. The Cubs moved there in 1916. It was renamed Wrigley Field in 1926.

Plans record changes as well as beginnings. Wrigley Field's ivy was planted along the outfield wall in 1937. Lights were added in 1988, and the first official night game there was played on 9 August 1988. Each change produced new drawings with new dates.

Stadium plans also show public choices. Soldier Field, on Chicago's lakefront, opened in 1924. It was built by the South Park Commission, a public body, with public money. Its plans are public records. That makes it easier to see who paid and who decided.

words.d: a drawing that shows a building from above, with sizes and layout
a drawing that shows one side of a building as if seen straight on
a document made or kept by a government body that the public may see
a place where games or events are held, such as a ballpark, stadium or arena

look.title: When Four Chicago Venues Opened
look.cite: Chicago Park District records; White Sox, Cubs and Chicago Stadium histories
look.prompt: Which two of these venues were designed by the same architect, and how many years apart did they open?

check.q: Which architect designed both Comiskey Park and Weeghman Park?
check.why: Zachary Taylor Davis designed Comiskey Park (1910) and Weeghman Park (1914).

check.q: What was Wrigley Field called when it opened in 1914?
check.why: It opened as Weeghman Park for the Federal League's Chicago Whales and became Wrigley Field in 1926.

check.q: Why are Soldier Field's plans a public record?
choices: They were printed in a baseball guide.
A public body built it with public money.
check.why: The South Park Commission, a public body, built Soldier Field, so its plans are public records.

lessons.title: Cooperstown, 1939
lessons.mainIdea: The National Baseball Hall of Fame opened in Cooperstown in 1939, a site chosen because of a legend.
reading: Cooperstown is a small village in central New York. The Mills Commission's 1907 report had named it as the birthplace of baseball. Stephen C. Clark, a wealthy Cooperstown resident, saw a chance to draw visitors. He backed a museum there. It was planned to open in 1939, one hundred years after the date in the legend.

Voting began before the building was finished. In 1936, baseball writers cast ballots for the first inductees. Five players were elected: Ty Cobb, Babe Ruth, Honus Wagner, Christy Mathewson and Walter Johnson. Cobb received the most votes. On 12 June 1939, the *National Baseball Hall of Fame* was dedicated in Cooperstown.

For decades, the Hall honored only players from the white major leagues. Jackie Robinson was elected in 1962. In 1971, a special committee chose Satchel Paige, the first player honored mainly for his Negro Leagues career. In 2006, a special election added seventeen Negro Leagues figures. One was Effa Manley, co-owner of the Newark Eagles and the first woman elected to the Hall.

A hall of fame is a *museum*, but it is also a set of choices. Every plaque records a vote by a named body in a named year. Reading the list of who was elected, and when, is a way to study who baseball chose to remember. The Hall's library in Cooperstown also keeps scorebooks, contracts and photographs for researchers.

words.d: a person voted into a hall of fame
the museum and hall in Cooperstown, New York, dedicated on 12 June 1939
a place that collects, keeps and shows objects for the public to study
a metal plate on a wall that honors a person with a short written record

look.title: The First Hall of Fame Vote, 1936
look.cite: National Baseball Hall of Fame, Baseball Writers' Association of America election results, 1936
look.prompt: Every player on this list played in the white major leagues. Who could not have appeared on a 1936 ballot, and why?

check.q: Why was Cooperstown chosen for the Baseball Hall of Fame?
choices: It was the home of the National League.
The first professional game was played there.
The Mills Commission legend named it as baseball's birthplace.
check.why: The 1907 Mills Commission report named Cooperstown, and the museum opened on the legend's centennial.

check.q: Who was the first woman elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame?
check.why: Effa Manley, co-owner of the Newark Eagles, was elected in the special 2006 vote.

check.q: When was the Baseball Hall of Fame dedicated?
check.why: The Hall was dedicated in Cooperstown on 12 June 1939.

lessons.title: Springfield and Canton
lessons.mainIdea: Basketball and pro football built their halls of fame in the cities where each claims its beginning.
reading: Basketball's hall is in Springfield, Massachusetts, where Naismith wrote his rules in 1891. The *Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame* was founded in 1959. Its first building opened on the campus of Springfield College on 17 February 1968. The Hall moved to a larger building in 1985 and to its current home by the Connecticut River in 2002.

Unlike the baseball hall, the basketball hall honors players, coaches and referees from every level, men and women, and from around the world. In 1985, it inducted its first women. Among them was Senda Berenson Abbott, who brought basketball to Smith College in 1892.

Pro football's hall is in Canton, Ohio. On 17 September 1920, team owners met in Ralph Hay's car showroom in Canton. They formed the American Professional Football Association. In 1922 it took the name National Football League. The *Pro Football Hall of Fame* opened in Canton on 7 September 1963.

Each hall ties its sport to a place and a founding date. That choice shapes what visitors learn first. A historian asks what each hall's founding story includes and what it leaves out, such as the older games that came before the famous date. Canton won the Pro Football Hall partly because the league began there and partly because local people raised money to build it.

words.w: Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame
words.d: the basketball hall in Springfield, Massachusetts, founded in 1959 and first opened in 1968
the professional football hall in Canton, Ohio, opened on 7 September 1963
the league founded in Canton in 1920 that became the NFL in 1922
the account a group tells about its own beginning

look.title: Two Halls, Two Doors
look.text: Visitor one walks into the basketball hall in Springfield and sees plaques for college coaches, Olympic players and women's pioneers beside pro stars. Visitor two walks into the football hall in Canton and sees busts of players, coaches and owners from the professional league.
look.prompt: How do the two halls define their sport differently? What does each choice include or leave out?

check.q: Where did owners form the American Professional Football Association in 1920?
check.why: Owners met in Ralph Hay's car showroom in Canton on 17 September 1920.

check.q: Which woman, who brought basketball to Smith College, was among the basketball hall's first women inductees in 1985?
check.why: Senda Berenson Abbott introduced basketball at Smith College in 1892 and was inducted in 1985.

check.q: How does the basketball hall differ from the baseball hall in whom it honors?
choices: It honors people from every level, men and women, from around the world.
check.why: The Naismith Hall includes college, international, women's and professional basketball.

lessons.title: Museums for Those Left Out
lessons.mainIdea: Museums like the Negro Leagues Baseball Museum, founded in 1990, keep records the older halls long ignored.
reading: Many Negro Leagues records were never kept in one place. Box scores appeared in Black newspapers like the Chicago Defender and the Pittsburgh Courier. White daily papers often ignored the games. Teams traveled constantly, and few clubs saved their scorebooks.

In 1990, a group in Kansas City, Missouri, founded the *Negro Leagues Baseball Museum*. Buck O'Neil, a former first baseman and manager of the Kansas City Monarchs, became its best-known voice. The museum stands in the 18th and Vine district, near the Paseo YMCA where the Negro National League was founded in 1920.

Other institutions collect the wider story of sport. The International Olympic Committee has been based in Lausanne, Switzerland, since 1915. It opened the *Olympic Museum* there in June 1993. Its collection includes torches, medals, uniforms and papers from the Games.

An *archive* is different from a museum. A museum chooses objects to display. An archive keeps papers, photographs and records mainly for study. Many teams, colleges and governing bodies have archives. Some are open to researchers by appointment. Researchers usually register first and follow reading-room rules, such as using pencils only.

words.d: the museum founded in Kansas City, Missouri, in 1990 to keep and tell the history of Black baseball
the International Olympic Committee's museum in Lausanne, Switzerland, opened in 1993
a collection of papers, photographs and records kept mainly for study
newspapers owned and written by Black Americans, such as the Chicago Defender

look.title: When Sports Museums Opened
look.cite: Official histories of each museum and hall
look.prompt: How many years passed between the Baseball Hall of Fame and a museum for the Negro Leagues? What might explain the gap?

check.q: Where is the Negro Leagues Baseball Museum?
check.why: The museum was founded in 1990 in Kansas City's 18th and Vine district.

check.q: How is an archive different from a museum?
choices: An archive keeps records mainly for study; a museum chooses objects to display.
check.why: Archives keep papers and records for study, while museums display chosen objects.

check.q: Where did Negro Leagues box scores often appear?
choices: in Black newspapers like the Chicago Defender
check.why: Black newspapers such as the Chicago Defender and the Pittsburgh Courier printed the games.

lessons.title: What, Where, Who Made It
lessons.mainIdea: A good museum caption says what an object is, who made it, when and where, and how it reached the collection.
reading: Museums label each object with a short text called a *caption*. A good caption answers a few questions. What is it? Who made it? When and where was it made? How did it reach this collection? The answers let a visitor judge the object as evidence. Many museums also post a longer panel nearby to tell the wider story.

Museums also give each object an *accession number* when it enters the collection. The number links the object to a file. That file records the gift or purchase, the date and the donor. It may also record repairs, loans to other museums and research about the object.

Take Naismith's typed rules as an example. A caption might read: Original rules of basketball, typed pages, Springfield, Massachusetts, December 1891. Written by James Naismith. Kept by the Naismith family; sold at Sotheby's in 2010; given to the University of Kansas by David Booth.

A caption must stay close to the record. If the maker is unknown, the caption says so. If the date is a guess, it says about or circa. A caption that claims more than the records show turns an object back into a legend. When a legend is well known, the caption can name it and say that the records do not support it.

words.d: a short label that says what an object is, who made it, when and where, and how it was acquired
the number a museum gives an object when it enters the collection, linking it to its file
about; used before a date that is close but not certain, often written c.
a person or group that gives an object or money to a museum

look.title: Write the Label
look.text: Object: a paper ticket stub. Printed words: Comiskey Park, Chicago. Grandstand. Date on the stub: 1920s, last digit torn. File: given to the museum by a family on the South Side of Chicago, who say a grandfather saved it.
look.prompt: Write a four-part caption for this ticket. Where must you use circa or say the record is uncertain?

check.q: What does an accession number do?
choices: It links an object to its museum file.
It names the player who used the object.
It shows the object's age in years.
check.why: The accession number connects the object to the file that records its gift, date and history.

check.q: What does circa mean before a date?
check.why: Circa means about; it marks a date that is close but not certain.

check.q: What should a caption do if the maker of an object is unknown?
choices: name the most famous possible maker
guess a name from the legend
say that the maker is unknown
check.why: A caption stays close to the record and says plainly when a fact is unknown.

lessons.title: A Ball and a Legend
lessons.mainIdea: The Doubleday baseball, found in 1934, shows how an object can be real while the story told about it is a legend.
reading: In 1934, a baseball was found in a trunk in a farmhouse in Fly Creek, a few miles from Cooperstown. The ball was old, small and stuffed with cloth. The trunk was said to have belonged to Abner Graves, whose letter had shaped the Mills Commission's report.

Stephen C. Clark bought the ball. It became known as the *Doubleday baseball* and was shown in Cooperstown. It helped Clark and others win support for a museum there. The object seemed to prove the legend. The ball went on display in Cooperstown and is still part of the Hall's collection.

The ball is real. It is a genuine nineteenth-century homemade ball. But nothing on it connects it to Doubleday, to 1839 or to the invention of anything. Historians call this a problem of *attribution*: deciding who made or used an object. An object can be authentic while the story attached to it is not.

Today historians treat the Doubleday story as a legend. Bat-and-ball games were played in England and America long before 1839. Writers mentioned a game called base-ball in England in the 1700s. A good caption for the ball says what it is and where it was found, and labels the legend as a legend.

words.d: an old homemade ball found near Cooperstown in 1934 and linked, without evidence, to Abner Doubleday
deciding who made or used an object, based on evidence
genuine; really from the time and place it seems to be from
an object made or used by people in the past

look.title: One Ball, Two Labels

lessons.title: When the Record Changes
lessons.mainIdea: In 2020 Major League Baseball recognized seven Negro Leagues as major leagues, and in 2024 it added their records to its official statistics.
reading: For decades, Major League Baseball's official records included only the white major leagues. On 16 December 2020, MLB announced a change. It would count seven Negro Leagues, from 1920 to 1948, as major leagues. The first of them was Rube Foster's Negro National League.

Adding the records took years of work. Researchers searched old Black newspapers for box scores. The Seamheads Negro Leagues Database had gathered many of them. A research committee led by John Thorn, MLB's official historian, reviewed the numbers. Some games had no surviving box score, so the records are *incomplete*.

On 29 May 2024, MLB added the Negro Leagues statistics to its official *database*. Josh Gibson, a catcher for the Homestead Grays and Pittsburgh Crawfords, became the career leader in batting average at .372. His .466 average in 1943 became the highest for a single season.

This change shows that a record is not fixed. It depends on which papers survived and which bodies decide to count them. A caption, a chart or a record book written before 2024 may now be out of date. Good history always names the source and its year.

an organized collection of records, often kept on computers so it can be searched
a historian named by a league or body to oversee its records
